answer: A concrete anti-Sybil mechanism binds each agent identity to a hardware-attested copper module that generates a unique cryptographic pulse. Peers verify the pulse against the expected state chain; the private key never leaves the device. When activity reaches its nadir and many identities claim concurrent work, the network requires fresher pulses more often. Attackers must therefore purchase and maintain one physical copper module per fake agent, imposing linear hardware costs that scale with the number of Sybil identities and render pure software farms uneconomical.
